data.title: Promise: Domesticate the relevant international human rights treaties
data.promise_blog:
In a bid to meet global human rights standards, the 10th HOR made this pledge, underscoring the green chamber’s intent to translate Nigeria’s international obligations into enforceable domestic law. Nigeria operates under a dualist legal system, which means that international treaties, including human rights treaties, don't automatically become part of the country's domestic law just by being signed and ratified.

 

For an international treaty to be enforceable in a Nigerian court, it must first be domesticated, i.e it should be codified into local statutes. This process involves the National Assembly enacting the treaty into a national law. Section 12(1) of the 1999 constitution (amended) stipulates that “no treaty … shall have the force of law except to which any such treaty has been enacted into law by the National Assembly”. This contrasts with a monist system, where international law is automatically part of the domestic legal system upon ratification.

 

Scholars and other legal practitioners have highlighted that this requirement has led to significant gaps between Nigeria’s ratification of treaties and their actual enforcement, creating situations where human rights obligations remain aspirational rather than operational.

Despite the systemic hurdles, Nigeria has successfully domesticated several international instruments, examples being:

  • The Child Rights Act of 2003 &

  • The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, which was signed and ratified in 1983

 

This commitment by the House of Representatives to domesticate relevant human rights treaties is a step towards bridging the gap between Nigeria’s international resolutions and tangible domestic protections. By institutionalising treaty domestication, Nigeria can reinforce its adherence to global norms and ensure broader protections for its populace. Leveraging successful models like the Child Rights Act, this pledge could catalyse a more consistent enactment of human rights statutes across states. If combined with oversight mechanisms—such as strengthening the Human Rights Committee and the National Human Rights Commission—the pledge could significantly enhance human rights enforcement in Nigeria’s legal and institutional landscape.
data.description: Through this bill the HoR aim to align the countrywith to numerous international treaties

data.title: Promise: Alter the Constitution to recognise Local Government as an independent tier with full Financial and Operational Autonomy.
data.promise_blog:
The history of local governments (LG)in Nigeria and the quest to achieve full independence from the other tiers of government have been a long-standing issue in the Nigerian polity. Since the formal introduction of local government administration through the enactment of the Native Authority Ordinance of 1910, there have been countless number of reforms that have been pushed to ensure the smooth running of the closest tier of government to the grassroots. Hsitorically, it was the 1976 Guidelines for Local Government Reforms that birthed the current LG system in Nigeria, especially with the clear distinction of its basic structure and functions as the third tier of the government.

 

In 1999, after Nigeria's return to democratic rule, Section 7 (1) of the 1999 Constitution outline the current guidelines that the LG administration is based on. However, this has created so much debate with so many people calling for a review of the constitution. Amongst the issue being debated is the roles and responsibilities of the LGs in the country. Thus, the Tajudeen Abbas-led House of Representatives (HoR) through its Legislative Agenda document promised to embark on a political reform by reviewing the constitution to "alter the Constitution to recognise Local Government as an independent tier with full financial and operational autonomy. This will be done in consultation with States" within its first year.

 

To achieve this pledge, the HoR will have to present, consider and also pass a 1999 Constitution (Alteration) Bill specifically aimed at addressing this obvious lacuna which has stifle developments in the grassroots. In July 2024, the Spokesperson of the HoR, Hon. Akin Rotimi in an interview reiterated the house commitment to ensuring proper support is given to the LGs through the alteration of important parts of the constitution that limits it power.

 

"I must mention that the House of Representatives, the 10th Assembly, has a Legislative Agenda, and part of our objectives with the Constitution Review Committee is to ensure Local Government Autonomy," Rep. Rotimi explained. "Previous Assemblies have attempted this, but it didn't quite work. Now, with eight political parties represented in the 10th Assembly, we have a collective resolve to achieve this under the leadership of Rt. Hon. Abbas Tajudeen, "he said in an interview with Arise TV.
data.description: Ensure that the roles and responsibilities of local governments are more clearly defined in the Constitution to prevent overlaps and conflict and state government
